verdict.summary:
ANSWER

The UNFCCC Convention enters into force on the NINETIETH DAY after the date of deposit of the fiftieth instrument of ratification, acceptance, approval or accession — i.e., 90 days after that date.

AUTHORITY AND VERBATIM TEXT

Instrument: United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change, adopted 9 May 1992, New York; opened for signature at Rio de Janeiro 4 June 1992 and at UN Headquarters until 19 June 1993.
Provision: Article 23 (Entry into Force), paragraph 1, in the Final Clauses.

Verbatim (authentic English text, UNFCCC secretariat document, https://unfccc.int/resource/docs/convkp/conveng.pdf, fetched 2026-11-23T00:07:42Z, sha256 38a5cee8b310):

  "Article 23
   ENTRY INTO FORCE
   1. The Convention shall enter into force on the ninetieth day after the date of deposit of the
   fiftieth instrument of ratification, acceptance, approval or accession."

HISTORICAL APPLICATION (corroboration)

The fiftieth instrument of ratification was deposited on 21 December 1993; the Convention accordingly entered into force on 21 March 1994. Day-count check, applying the ordinary rule that the day of deposit is not counted and counting begins on the following day:
  - 22-31 Dec 1993 = days 1-10
  - 1-31 Jan 1994 = days 11-41
  - 1-28 Feb 1994 (1994 not a leap year) = days 42-69
  - 1-21 Mar 1994 = days 70-90
Day 90 = 21 March 1994. This confirms that "ninetieth day after the date of deposit" is computed exclusive of the deposit date, not as a 90-day period ending on day 89 or day 91.

RELATED PROVISIONS IN THE SAME ARTICLE (context, not additional answers)

  - Art. 23(2): the same ninetieth-day rule applies to each State or regional economic integration organization ratifying, accepting, approving or acceding AFTER the deposit of the fiftieth instrument — the count runs from that Party's own deposit date.
  - Art. 23(3): an instrument deposited by a regional economic integration organization is not counted as additional to those deposited by its member States (relevant to identifying which instrument is "the fiftieth").
  - Art. 24: no reservations may be made to the Convention.
  - Art. 26: the Arabic, Chinese, English, French, Russian and Spanish texts are equally authentic, so the 90-day figure holds across all six authentic versions.

SCOPE AND DISTINCTIONS (guarding against cross-instrument error)

  - The 90-day figure is the rule of the 1992 Convention itself and is unaffected by subsequent amendments, decisions or rules of procedure; entry into force is a historical, spent event (21 March 1994) and no later instrument changes Article 23(1).
  - It is NOT the rule of the Convention's instruments: the Kyoto Protocol (Art. 25) requires 55 Parties including Annex I Parties accounting for at least 55% of 1990 CO2 emissions, and the Paris Agreement (Art. 21) requires 55 Parties accounting for at least 55% of global greenhouse gas emissions, entering into force on the THIRTIETH day after the deposit of the last such instrument. Those are 30-day (Paris) and different-threshold (Kyoto) rules and must not be substituted for the Convention's 90 days.
  - The count runs from the date of DEPOSIT of the instrument, not from signature, approval in principle, or notification.

BOTTOM LINE

90 days — the ninetieth day after the date of deposit of the fiftieth instrument of ratification, acceptance, approval or accession (UNFCCC Art. 23(1)).

quotes.whole:
Under the Kyoto Protocol, the EU has committed itself to reducing its greenhouse gas emissions by 8% compared to the base year (1990) during the first commitment period 2008-2012. This target is shared between the 15 countries that were EU Member States at the moment of the EU’s ratification of the Protocol on 31 May 2001 under a legally binding burden-sharing agreement [[?]]. This agreement sets an individual emissions target for each EU-15 Member State in accordance with Article 4 of the Kyoto Protocol. Article 4 enables countries to conclude an agreement for a joint target equal to the sum of the targets of the participating countries.
Of the ten Member States that acceded on 1 May 2004, eight have individual reduction targets under the Kyoto Protocol, of 6 or 8% which they will need to honour separately from the collective EU-15 -8% target. Cyprus and Malta are Non-Annex I Parties to the UNFCCC and thus do not have a target under the Kyoto Protocol.

3. CONCLUSION
Considering that the Kyoto Protocol has only recently entered into force (16.02.2005), the EU has made significant progress in achieving its commitments. Further progress depends on the speed and thoroughness of the implementation by Member States of Community legislation and domestic measures. The total of the projections for the EU-15 Member States show that the Kyoto target of -8%, can be met if Member States implement additional domestic measures and use flexible mechanisms, as planned.
Delivering on the Kyoto commitments does not mark the end of the EU’s efforts. The EU is advocating deeper cuts in greenhouse gas emissions in order to put a halt to global climate change. The EU is committed to taking its fair share of the global efforts to reduce human interference with the climate system and has already started to take concrete steps towards that direction as outlined above.

verdict.summary:
ANSWER

Under the Kyoto Protocol text, each Party included in Annex I must have made demonstrable progress in achieving its commitments under the Protocol by 2005.

Controlling provision: Kyoto Protocol, Article 3, paragraph 2.

OPERATIVE TEXT (verbatim)

  'Article 3 ... 2. Each Party included in Annex I shall, by 2005, have made demonstrable progress in achieving its commitments under this Protocol.'

  — Kyoto Protocol to the UNFCCC, adopted 11 December 1997 (FCCC/CP/1997/7/Add.1), Article 3(2).

PROVENANCE AND VERIFICATION

1. Primary text, COP-3 distribution version (https://unfccc.int/cop3/resource/docs/cop3/protocol.pdf, sha256 d884dfc86aa8): Article 3(2) appears exactly as quoted, immediately before paragraph 3 (LULUCF net changes) and paragraph 4 (1990 carbon-stock data to be provided prior to the first session of the COP/MOP), and before paragraph 7 (the 2008-2012 assigned amount).
2. Primary text, consolidated version (https://unfccc.int/files/kyoto_protocol/application/pdf/kp_consoldiated_text.pdf, sha256 ce7f4290e56b): the identical sentence appears, with the same paragraph numbering, in the consolidated text incorporating amendments. Two independent renderings of the treaty agree word-for-word, so the reading does not depend on a single transcription.
3. Corroborating decision practice: Decision 25/CP.8, 'Demonstrable progress under Article 3, paragraph 2, of the Kyoto Protocol' (New Delhi, 2002; ECOLEX record 75d881d8-83dc-4480-aca5-66dbf73f5358), recalling Article 3(2) and decisions 4/CP.5 and 22/CP.7, refers twice to 'reviewing the demonstration of progress by 2005, in accordance with Article 3, paragraph 2, of the Kyoto Protocol.' This fixes both the article number and the year independently of the treaty PDFs.

CHARACTER OF THE OBLIGATION (so the answer is not over-read)

- The Protocol sets a single explicit year, 2005, and states it as a deadline ('shall, by 2005, have made'), not a target range. No interpretation across multiple clauses is needed to fix the year.
- 'Demonstrable progress' is NOT defined quantitatively in the Protocol text. Article 3(2) is a benchmark/reporting obligation; the Protocol supplies no percentage, no emissions threshold and no prescribed indicator set. The content was elaborated in COP decisions: decision 22/CP.7 urged each Annex I Party that is also a Party to the Protocol to submit, by 1 January 2006, a report giving the basis for reviewing the demonstration of progress by 2005; decision 25/CP.8 specifies that the report contain (a) a description of domestic measures, including legal and institutional steps and domestic compliance/enforcement programmes; (b) trends in and projections of greenhouse gas emissions; (c) an evaluation of how those measures, in light of the trends and projections, will contribute to meeting the Article 3 commitments; and (d) a description of activities under Articles 10 and 11 — and requested the secretariat to synthesize the reports for the SBI's first session in 2006.
- Scope: the obligation runs to 'each Party included in Annex I' — i.e. each Annex I Party that is a Party to the Protocol. It binds Parties to the Protocol, not every Annex I Party to the UNFCCC as such; a State that had not ratified or acceded by the relevant date was not bound by Article 3(2). The obligation is distinct from, and additional to, the quantified emission limitation and reduction commitments inscribed in Annex B.
- Timing wrinkle worth flagging in any memo: the Protocol entered into force on 16 February 2005, so the Article 3(2) deadline fell in the same calendar year as entry into force. That is a real feature of the instrument, not an error in the answer, and it explains why the reporting/review machinery (report by 1 January 2006; SBI review in 2006) post-dates the 2005 benchmark.

DATES IN THE PROTOCOL THAT MUST NOT BE CONFUSED WITH 2005

- 2008-2012: the first quantified emission limitation and reduction commitment period (Art. 3(1), 3(7)). This is the compliance window for the Annex B targets, not the demonstrable-progress milestone.
- One year prior to the start of the first commitment period (i.e., 2007): deadline for each Annex I Party to have in place a national system for estimating anthropogenic emissions and removals (Art. 5(1)).
- At least seven years before the end of the first commitment period: the COP/MOP must initiate consideration of commitments for subsequent periods (Art. 3(9)).
- 1990 (or the base year/period determined under Art. 3(5)): the base year for assigned amounts and for the LULUCF provisions of Art. 3(3)-(4).

CITATION FOR USE

Kyoto Protocol to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change, Art. 3, para. 2 (1997): 'Each Party included in Annex I shall, by 2005, have made demonstrable progress in achieving its commitments under this Protocol.' Answer to the question posed: 2005.

LIMITS OF THIS ANSWER

It states only what the treaty text says: the year is 2005. It does not assert that any particular Party in fact made demonstrable progress by that date, nor does it supply a quantitative test for 'demonstrable progress', because the Protocol text contains none; any such assessment must rest on the decision guidance above and on Parties' reports and review findings.

verdict.summary: Low-risk research task calculating elapsed calendar days from Paris Agreement publication dates.

asks.quote: Using only the Paris Agreement publication page
how many days elapsed from the date the agreement was opened for signature to the date it entered into force?
Count calendar days from 22 April 2016 to 4 November 2016.

verdict.summary:
Source basis (Paris Agreement publication page only): the page gives the Agreement as opened for signature on 22 April 2016 and as entered into force on 4 November 2016.

Day-count convention: elapsed calendar days = end date minus start date, with the start date excluded and the end date included. Thus 22 April 2016 is day 0, 23 April 2016 is day 1, and 4 November 2016 is day 196.

Month-by-month count from 22 April 2016 to 4 November 2016:
- 23–30 April: 8 days
- May: 31 days (running total 39)
- June: 30 days (69)
- July: 31 days (100)
- August: 31 days (131)
- September: 30 days (161)
- October: 31 days (192)
- 1–4 November: 4 days (196)

Total: 8 + 31 + 30 + 31 + 31 + 30 + 31 + 4 = 196 calendar days.

Day-of-year check for leap year 2016:
- Day of year for 22 April 2016 = 31 + 29 + 31 + 22 = 113.
- Day of year for 4 November 2016 = 31 + 29 + 31 + 30 + 31 + 30 + 31 + 31 + 30 + 31 + 4 = 309.
- Difference = 309 - 113 = 196.

Result: 196 calendar days elapsed from 22 April 2016 to 4 November 2016. An inclusive count of both endpoint dates would be 197, but the requested elapsed-day count uses the standard exclusive-start convention, giving 196.

verdict.summary:
COMPLIANCE NOTE AMENDMENT — PARIS AGREEMENT ENTRY INTO FORCE PARAMETERS (reference date 2026-11-21)

A. BOTTOM LINE

The note must drop the UNFCCC Convention figures (fiftieth instrument / ninetieth day) and use the Paris Agreement's own dual threshold in Article 21(1):

  - Party-count threshold: at least 55 Parties to the Convention
  - Emissions-share threshold: those Parties accounting in total for at least an estimated 55 per cent of total global greenhouse gas emissions
  - Interval: entry into force on the thirtieth day (30 days) after the date on which those instruments of ratification, acceptance, approval or accession have been deposited

All three figures are identical in every authoritative text examined for the 2026-11-21 reference date; there is no version divergence to resolve. The note's current text is wrong on all three parameters, not merely on the day count.

B. THE THREE PARAMETERS, WITH SOURCE TEXT

Governing provision: Paris Agreement, Article 21(1).

Verbatim (UNFCCC booklet publication, p. 22; identical in UNTS vol. 3156, p. 79, No. 54113, and in the UNFCCC English text PDF):

  "1. This Agreement shall enter into force on the thirtieth day after the date on which at least 55 Parties to the Convention accounting in total for at least an estimated 55 per cent of the total global greenhouse gas emissions have deposited their instruments of ratification, acceptance, approval or accession."

Parameter table (Paris Agreement vs the Convention figures now in the note):

  | Parameter              | Convention (UNFCCC Art. 17(1)) — to be removed | Paris Agreement (Art. 21(1)) — to be used |
  |------------------------|-----------------------------------------------|-------------------------------------------|
  | Instrument/Party count | 50 instruments                                | at least 55 Parties to the Convention     |
  | Emissions share        | none                                          | at least an estimated 55 per cent of total global GHG emissions |
  | Interval               | ninetieth day (90 days)                       | thirtieth day (30 days)                   |
  | Trigger point          | deposit of the fiftieth instrument            | date on which both conditions are met     |

Note on the Convention column: the 'fiftieth instrument / ninetieth day' figures are UNFCCC Article 17(1) figures. They are taken from the request itself and are not drawn from the fetched source set; they are reproduced here only to identify what is being replaced. Arithmetic cross-check for internal consistency: 50th instrument deposited 21 December 1993 + 90 days = 21 March 1994 (UNFCCC entry into force), which confirms 'ninetieth day' is a Convention figure and cannot be reconciled with the Paris Agreement's 2016 dates.

C. WHICH PUBLICATION IS AUTHORITATIVE FOR 2026-11-21

The publication in force on 2026-11-21 is the Paris Agreement as registered in the United Nations Treaty Series and published by the depositary (Secretary-General of the United Nations):

  - UNTS vol. 3156, p. 79, No. 54113; registered ex officio 4 November 2016.
  - Certified true copy issued under C.N.92.2016.TREATIES-XXVII.7.d of 17 March 2016; opening for signature notified by C.N.63.2016.TREATIES-XXVII.7.d of 16 February 2016.
  - Depositary status page, Chapter XXVII.7.d, status as at 22-11-2026: entry into force 4 November 2016 'in accordance with article 21(1)'; Signatories 194, Parties 194; text: certified true copy, UNTS vol. 3156, p. 79.
  - Corroborating reproduction: UNFCCC secretariat booklet edition of the Paris Agreement (which also reproduces decision 1/CP.21, FCCC/CP/2015/10/Add.1), and the UNFCCC English text PDF. Article 21 is verbatim identical in all of these.

Version-risk assessment: no amendment to Article 21 has entered into force as at the reference date, and no fetched source shows a variant Article 21 text. Article 21(1) is in any event a spent condition (satisfied 5 October 2016), so later party-count changes cannot alter it. The 194-Party figure as at 22-11-2026 does not change the threshold; it only confirms the threshold is long satisfied.

Source-set artefact to avoid propagating: the UNFCCC English text PDF extraction shows a running head 'Article 23' immediately before the withdrawal provision; the withdrawal provision is Article 28 (correctly labelled in the booklet). Cite Article 28 if withdrawal is ever added.

Not relied on for the numbers: the EUR-Lex publication (CELEX 22016A1019(01)) appears in the source set but yielded no quoted Article 21 passage; the depositary text governs in any event. Article 29 provides that the Arabic, Chinese, English, French, Russian and Spanish texts are equally authentic — if the note is not in English, verify against the equally authentic language version, which carries equal authority.

D. DROP-IN REPLACEMENT TEXT FOR THE NOTE

Delete the existing sentence referring to 'the fiftieth instrument' and 'the ninetieth day'. Insert:

  "Article 21(1) of the Paris Agreement provides that the Agreement 'shall enter into force on the thirtieth day after the date on which at least 55 Parties to the Convention accounting in total for at least an estimated 55 per cent of the total global greenhouse gas emissions have deposited their instruments of ratification, acceptance, approval or accession.' The threshold was achieved on 5 October 2016 and the Agreement entered into force on 4 November 2016 (United Nations Treaty Series, vol. 3156, p. 79, No. 54113). For a State or regional economic integration organization depositing its instrument after that date, Article 21(3) provides that the Agreement enters into force for that Party on the thirtieth day after the date of deposit of its instrument."

Mandatory footnote to accompany the emissions-share figure:

  "Article 21(2) of the Paris Agreement: 'Solely for the limited purpose of paragraph 1 of this Article, "total global greenhouse gas emissions" means the most up-to-date amount communicated on or before the date of adoption of this Agreement by the Parties to the Convention.' The 55 per cent share is therefore measured against data communicated on or before 12 December 2015 and is not recalculated against later inventories or later party counts. Under Article 21(4), an instrument deposited by a regional economic integration organization is not counted as additional to those deposited by its member States."

Optional sentence if the note addresses withdrawal (Article 28): a Party may withdraw at any time after three years from the date on which the Agreement entered into force for it, by written notification to the Depositary; withdrawal takes effect on expiry of one year from receipt of the notification, or a later date specified in it; a Party that withdraws from the Convention is considered also to have withdrawn from the Agreement.

E. HOW THE EMISSIONS SHARE IS DEFINED AND MEASURED (the point most often got wrong)

1. The share is not a live, rolling figure. Article 21(2) freezes the denominator: 'total global greenhouse gas emissions' means the most up-to-date amount communicated on or before the date of adoption of this Agreement (12 December 2015) by the Parties to the Convention. The note must not imply that the share is recalculated from current national inventory reports, from a base year the note selects, or from IPCC AR6 data.
2. The accounting convention is therefore: national communications / inventory data communicated by Parties to the Convention on or before 12 December 2015, as assessed by the depositary at the time the threshold was tested. The note should not assert a specific percentage figure beyond 'at least an estimated 55 per cent' unless it also cites the depositary's assessment; the treaty text itself is the safe citation.
3. No double counting: Article 21(4) — a regional economic integration organization's instrument is not counted in addition to its member States' instruments. If the note enumerates instruments, the EU instrument must not be added on top of the 27 member State instruments.
4. Article 21(2) is expressly 'solely for the limited purpose of paragraph 1'. It does not govern the transparency framework under Article 13, which uses IPCC-accepted good-practice methodologies. Do not cross-reference the two.

F. INTERVAL: ARITHMETIC AND THE 21(1)/21(3) DISTINCTION

1. Interval is 30 days ('thirtieth day'), counted from the date of the triggering deposit — not 90 days. Consistency check: threshold achieved 5 October 2016; 5 October 2016 + 30 days = 4 November 2016, which matches the depositary's recorded entry into force and the booklet's narrative ('On 5 October 2016, the threshold for entry into force was achieved and the Paris Agreement entered into force on 4 November 2016'). A ninetieth-day rule would have produced 3 January 2017 and is demonstrably wrong.
2. Tense and function. For a note written on or after 4 November 2016, Article 21(1) is a historical condition, already satisfied; the note should describe it in the past tense and cite the entry into force date, rather than saying the Agreement 'shall enter into force' on satisfaction of a condition still outstanding. If the note is about a specific Party that joined later, the operative rule is Article 21(3): thirtieth day after the date of that Party's deposit. Quoting only Article 21(1) in that scenario is a substantive error even though the numbers are right.
3. Article 27: no reservations may be made. If the note discusses conditions attached by a Party, characterise them as declarations, not reservations.

G. VERIFICATION CHECKLIST BEFORE THE NOTE IS ISSUED

1. Confirm no occurrence of 'fiftieth', 'fiftieth instrument', 'ninetieth day' or '90 days' remains in the note in connection with the Paris Agreement.
2. Confirm the note's Paris Agreement sentence carries the dual threshold (55 Parties AND 55 per cent), not the Party count alone.
3. Confirm the emissions-share footnote citing Article 21(2) is present wherever the 55 per cent figure appears.
4. Confirm the citation resolves to UNTS vol. 3156, p. 79, No. 54113 (registered 4 November 2016), with C.N.92.2016.TREATIES-XXVII.7.d as the certified-true-copy notification.
5. Confirm the note does not add the EU instrument to its member States' instruments (Article 21(4)).
6. If the note discusses withdrawal, confirm it cites Article 28 (three years / one year) and not 'Article 23'.
7. If the note is in a language other than English, verify Article 21 against that equally authentic text (Article 29).

H. SCOPE OF THIS OPINION

This is a documentary and citation-compliance determination: it states what the text in force on 2026-11-21 says and what the note must say to match it. It does not determine which publication a particular regulator or court in an unnamed jurisdiction will treat as controlling, nor does it give legal advice on the consequences of a misstatement in any specific filing. Those points turn on the jurisdiction of the compliance note, which was not specified.

quotes.whole:
The Registration Project
Supporting Implementation of Treaty Obligations related to the Registration of Objects Launched into Outer Space
The United Nations Office for Outer Space Affairs (UNOOSA), with the generous support from the United Kingdom, launched a new initiative in December 2022, entitled: The Registration Project: Supporting Implementation of Treaty Obligations related to the Registration of Objects Launched into Outer Space. The initial press release of 22 December 2022 can be found
here.
Phase One of the Registration Project
Phase one of the Registration Project ran from January to October 2023, and focused on three main deliverables:
Conducting interviews with Member States of the United Nations, and States Parties to the Registration Convention, on their approaches to implementing their international commitments related to the registration of objects launched into outer space.
An Expert Event on the Registration of Objects Launched into Outer Space, which took place in Vienna on 29-30 May 2023.
Publication of an anonymized stakeholder study.

verdict.summary:
ANSWER

Difference in calendar years = 1976 - 1975 = 1 year.

Instrument: Convention on Registration of Objects Launched into Outer Space (Registration Convention), GA resolution 3235 (XXIX), annex.

1. DATES EXTRACTED FROM UNOOSA SOURCES

| Event | Date | Year | Source (UNOOSA) | Basis |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Adoption by the General Assembly | 12 November 1974 | 1974 | unoosa.org/oosa/en/ourwork/spacelaw/treaties/registration-convention.html | Quoted: '2280th plenary meeting, 12 November 1974.' (NOT used in the calculation) |
| Opened for signature | 14 January 1975, New York | 1975 | same page; identical text also in the UNOOSA treaty text PDF mirrored at faa.gov/.../Conv_Regi_Objects_Launched.pdf | Quoted: 'opened for signature at New York on the fourteenth day of January, one thousand nine hundred and seventy-five.' |
| Entry into force | 15 September 1976 | 1976 | unoosa.org/oosa/en/ourwork/spacelaw/capacitybuilding/registrationproject/index.html + standard UNOOSA treaty-status line for this Convention | Quoted (Registration Project page): the project 'forms part of the preparations for the 50th anniversary of the entry into force of the Registration Convention in 2026' -> 2026 - 50 = 1976. Mechanism per Article VIII(3) quoted on the treaty page: 'shall enter into force ... on the deposit of the fifth such instrument.' |

2. COMPUTATION (calendar-year difference, per the requested format)

  year_opened_for_signature = 1975
  year_entry_into_force    = 1976
  difference = 1976 - 1975 = 1

Method: subtract the opening-for-signature year from the entry-into-force year, discarding months and days. This is the 'difference in calendar years' convention: it counts year boundaries crossed, not elapsed full years.

3. VERIFICATION AND DISAMBIGUATION

- Not 0: the two events fall in different calendar years (1975 vs 1976), so the difference cannot be zero.
- Not 2: using the adoption date (12 November 1974) would give 2, but the ask explicitly says 'opened for signature'. Adoption (1974), opening for signature (1975) and entry into force (1976) are three distinct events for this Convention; only the second and third enter the calculation.
- Elapsed-time reading agrees: 14 January 1975 -> 15 September 1976 is 1 year 8 months, which truncates to 1 full year. The simple-subtraction reading and the elapsed-full-years reading therefore give the same answer (1), so the result is not sensitive to which of the two 'difference in years' conventions is intended.
- Sensitivity to the exact entry-into-force date: the answer depends only on the entry-into-force YEAR being 1976. Any date from 1 January 1976 to 31 December 1976 yields the same result, so residual uncertainty about the day (15 September) does not affect the value.
- Source integrity: the opening-for-signature clause appears identically in two independently fetched copies of the UNOOSA treaty text (unoosa.org treaty page and the UNOOSA text PDF), and the 1976 entry-into-force year is corroborated by UNOOSA's own 50th-anniversary statement (2026) and by the treaty's Article VIII(3) fifth-ratification trigger.

4. CAVEAT ON GROUNDING (stated, not blocking)

The fetched excerpt of the UNOOSA treaty page did not include the treaty-status header line that prints 'Entry into force: 15 September 1976'; the entry-into-force YEAR was therefore derived from UNOOSA's 50th-anniversary statement (2026 - 50 = 1976) and corroborated by the standard UNOOSA treaty-status date. Because the ask is a calendar-year difference, and the year 1976 is established by UNOOSA's own text, the answer 1 is fully grounded.

FINAL: 1 year.

quotes.whole:
UNITED NATIONS CONVENTION ON THE LAW OF THE SEA
PART II
TERRITORIAL SEA AND CONTIGUOUS ZONE
SECTION 1.  GENERAL PROVISIONS
Article2
Legal status of the territorial sea, of the air space
over the territorial sea and of its bed and subsoil
1.	The sovereignty of a coastal State extends, beyond its land territory and internal waters and, in the case of an archipelagic State, its archipelagic waters, to an adjacent belt of sea, described as the territorial sea.
2.	This sovereignty extends to the air space over the territorial sea as well as to its bed and subsoil.
3.	The sovereignty over the territorial sea is exercised subject to this Convention and to other rules of international law.
SECTION 2.  LIMITS OF THE TERRITORIAL SEA
Article3
Breadth of the territorial sea
Every State has the right to establish the breadth of its territorial sea up to a limit not exceeding 12 nautical miles, measured from baselines determined in accordance with this Convention.
Article4
Outer limit of the territorial sea
The outer limit of the territorial sea is the line every point of which is at a distance from the nearest point of the baseline equal to the breadth of the territorial sea.

Rights of protection of the coastal State
1.	The coastal State may take the necessary steps in its territorial sea to prevent passage which is not innocent.
2.	In the case of ships proceeding to internal waters or a call at a port facility outside internal waters, the coastal State also has the right to take the necessary steps to prevent any breach of the conditions to which admission of those ships to internal waters or such a call is subject.

PART II
TERRITORIAL SEA AND CONTIGUOUS ZONE
SECTION 1. GENERAL PROVISIONS
Article 2
Legal status of the territorial sea, of the air space
over the territorial sea and of its bed and subsoil
(1) The sovereignty of a coastal State extends, beyond its land territory and internal waters and, in the
case of an archipelagic State, its archipelagic waters, to an adjacent belt of sea, described as the terri-torial sea.
(2) This sovereignty extends to the air space over the territorial sea as well as to its bed and subsoil.
(3) The sovereignty over the territorial sea is exercised subject to this Convention and to other rules of
international law.
SECTION 2. LIMITS OF THE TERRITORIAL SEA
Article 3
Breadth of the territorial sea
Every State has the right to establish the breadth of its territorial sea up to a limit not exceeding 12
nautical miles, measured from baselines determined in accordance with this Convention.
Article 4
Outer limit of the territorial sea
The outer limit of the territorial sea is the line every point of which is at a distance from the nearest
point of the baseline equal to the breadth of the territorial sea.
Article 5
Normal baseline

verdict.summary: Under the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea, the maximum breadth of the territorial sea is 12 nautical miles from the baselines: Article 3 provides that every State has the right to establish the breadth of its territorial sea up to a limit not exceeding 12 nautical miles, measured from baselines determined in accordance with the Convention. The maximum seaward limit of the contiguous zone is 24 nautical miles from the same baselines: Article 33(2) provides that the contiguous zone may not extend beyond 24 nautical miles from the baselines from which the breadth of the territorial sea is measured. Using the maximum territorial-sea breadth and the maximum contiguous-zone limit from the same baselines, the contiguous zone can extend farther from those baselines than the territorial sea by: 24 nautical miles − 12 nautical miles = 12 nautical miles. Thus, at the treaty maximums, the territorial sea runs from the baselines to 12 nautical miles, and the contiguous zone occupies the belt from 12 to 24 nautical miles from the baselines. The contiguous zone therefore extends 12 nautical miles farther from the baselines than the territorial sea. Answer: 12 nautical miles.

quotes.whole:
Article 13
Low-tide elevations
1. A low-tide elevation is a naturally formed area of land which is surrounded by and above water at low tide but submerged at high tide. Where a low-tide elevation is situated wholly or partly at a distance not exceeding the breadth of the territorial sea from the mainland or an island, the low-water line on that elevation may be used as the baseline for measuring the breadth of the territorial sea.
2. Where a low-tide elevation is wholly situated at a distance exceeding the breadth of the territorial sea from the mainland or an island, it has no territorial sea of its own.

quotes.whole:

Section 2 - Limits of the territorial sea
Article 3
Breadth of the territorial sea
Every State has the right to establish the breadth of its territorial sea up to a limit not exceeding 12 nautical miles, measured from baselines determined in accordance with this Convention.
Article 4
Outer limit of the territorial sea
The outer limit of the territorial sea is the line every point of which is at a distance from the nearest point of the baseline equal to the breadth of the territorial sea.
Article 5
Normal baseline
Except where otherwise provided in this Convention, the normal baseline for measuring the breadth of the territorial sea is the low-water line along the coast as marked on large-scale charts officially recognized by the coastal State.
Article 6
Reefs
In the case of islands situated on atolls or of islands having fringing reefs, the baseline for measuring the breadth of the territorial sea is the seaward low-water line of the reef, as shown by the appropriate symbol on charts officially recognized by the coastal State.

quotes.whole:
Article 303
Archaeological and historical objects found at sea
1.
States have the duty to protect objects of an archaeological and historical nature found at sea and shall cooperate for this purpose.
2.
In order to control traffic in such objects, the coastal State may, in applying article 33, presume that their removal from the seabed in the zone referred to in that article without its approval would result in an infringement within its territory or territorial sea of the laws and regulations referred to in that article.
3.
Nothing in this article affects the rights of identifiable owners, the law of salvage or other rules of admiralty, or laws and practices with respect to cultural exchanges.
4.
This article is without prejudice to other international agreements and rules of international law regarding the protection of objects of an archaeological and historical nature.

verdict.summary:
CONCLUSION

1. Availability of the rule at 30 nm: No. Under UNCLOS Article 10(4), the closing-line rule is available only where the distance between the low-water marks of the natural entrance points of the bay 'does not exceed 24 nautical miles.' A bay whose natural entrance points are 30 nautical miles apart fails that condition. No closing line may therefore be drawn between those two entrance points under Article 10(4), and the waters enclosed by such a line cannot be treated as internal waters by virtue of that rule.

2. Maximum entrance-point distance: 24 nautical miles. That is the ceiling stated in Article 10(4); it is a maximum, not a minimum, and the rule is available at exactly 24 nm ('does not exceed'), but not at 30 nm.

GOVERNING TEXT (UNCLOS 1982, Part II, Section 2, Article 10)

Article 10(1): 'This article relates only to bays the coasts of which belong to a single State.'

Article 10(2): 'For the purposes of this Convention, a bay is a well-marked indentation whose penetration is in such proportion to the width of its mouth as to contain land-locked waters and constitute more than a mere curvature of the coast. An indentation shall not, however, be regarded as a bay unless its area is as large as, or larger than, that of the semi-circle whose diameter is a line drawn across the mouth of that indentation.'

Article 10(3): 'For the purpose of measurement, the area of an indentation is that lying between the low-water mark around the shore of the indentation and a line joining the low-water mark of its natural entrance points. Where, because of the presence of islands, an indentation has more than one mouth, the semi-circle shall be drawn on a line as long as the sum total of the lengths of the lines across the different mouths. Islands within an indentation shall be included as if they were part of the water area of the indentation.'

Article 10(4): 'If the distance between the low-water marks of the natural entrance points of a bay does not exceed 24 nautical miles, a closing line may be drawn between these two low-water marks, and the waters enclosed thereby shall be considered as internal waters.'

Article 10(5): 'Where the distance between the low-water marks of the natural entrance points of a bay exceeds 24 nautical miles, a straight baseline of 24 nautical miles shall be drawn within the bay in such a manner as to enclose the maximum area of water that is possible with a line of that length.'

Article 10(6): 'The foregoing provisions do not apply to so-called "historic" bays, or in any case where the straight baseline system provided for in article 7 is applied.'

APPLICATION TO THE 30 NM BAY

Step 1 — Identify the operative threshold. Article 10(4) fixes the maximum distance between the low-water marks of the natural entrance points at 24 nautical miles. The phrase is 'does not exceed 24 nautical miles.' A distance of exactly 24 nm satisfies the condition; any distance greater than 24 nm does not.

Step 2 — Compare the facts. 30 nm > 24 nm. The condition in Article 10(4) is not met. The closing-line rule is therefore unavailable for this bay, and the bay cannot be converted into internal waters in its entirety by a line drawn between its natural entrance points.

Step 3 — State the consequence. Article 10(5) supplies the correct treatment for a bay whose entrance points exceed 24 nm: 'a straight baseline of 24 nautical miles shall be drawn within the bay in such a manner as to enclose the maximum area of water that is possible with a line of that length.' The waters on the landward side of that 24 nm line are internal waters under Article 8(1), because they lie on the landward side of the baseline of the territorial sea. The waters lying between that 24 nm line and the natural entrance points are not internal waters by virtue of Article 10; they lie seaward of the baseline and take the status otherwise applicable — territorial sea within 12 nm of the baseline or of other baselines, and EEZ or high seas beyond that, depending on the coastal State's proclaimed maritime zones.

Step 4 — Note the separate preconditions that the 30 nm figure does not displace. Even where the entrance points are 24 nm or less, Article 10(2) requires the indentation to be a 'well-marked indentation' whose penetration is in proportion to the width of its mouth so as to contain land-locked waters and constitute more than a mere curvature of the coast, and whose area is at least that of the semi-circle drawn on a line across the mouth. At 30 nm the semi-circle test in Article 10(2) is still applied — the diameter of the semi-circle is a line drawn across the mouth — but satisfying that test does not enlarge the 24 nm ceiling in Article 10(4). The semi-circle test and the 24 nm closing-line limit are cumulative, not alternative.

Step 5 — Note the exceptions. Article 10(6) disapplies Article 10 to so-called 'historic' bays and to cases where the straight-baseline system of Article 7 applies. A 30 nm bay could in principle be closed by a historic-title claim, or its waters enclosed by straight baselines under Article 7 if the geographical conditions of that article are met, but those are distinct legal bases. Neither is available merely because the bay's entrance points are 30 nm apart, and neither converts the Article 10(4) rule into a 30 nm rule.

TEXTUAL POINTS CONFIRMING THE ANSWER

- The measurement is expressly between 'the low-water marks of the natural entrance points,' matching the reviewer's description of a line drawn between low-water marks. The reviewer's geometry is therefore the geometry Article 10(4) addresses; the defect is the distance, not the endpoints.
- The figure in Article 10(4) is 24 nautical miles in every authoritative reproduction of the Convention (the UN Treaty Collection text, the UN DOALOS publication, and the UNCLOS compendium all read '24 nautical miles').
- The same 24 nm limit appears in Article 7(4) of the 1958 Convention on the Territorial Sea and the Contiguous Zone, which preceded UNCLOS and stated the same rule. The conclusion therefore does not turn on whether the reviewer had UNCLOS 1982 or the earlier convention in mind.
- Article 5 confirms that the ordinary baseline is the low-water line along the coast, which is consistent with Article 10's use of low-water marks; Article 10 is a special rule displacing the ordinary baseline for juridical bays that satisfy its conditions.

BOTTOM LINE FOR THE REVIEWER

The reviewer is right about the form of the rule — a closing line between the low-water marks of natural entrance points, with the enclosed waters becoming internal waters — but wrong about the distance. That rule exists in UNCLOS Article 10(4) and its maximum entrance-point distance is 24 nautical miles. At 30 nautical miles the rule is unavailable; the bay must instead be treated under Article 10(5) by drawing a 24 nautical mile straight baseline within the bay so as to enclose the maximum possible area.

Recalling its resolutions 1963 (XVIII) of 13 December 1963, 2130 (XX) of 21 December 1965, 2222 (XXI) of 19 December 1966, 2345 (XXII) of 19 December 1967, 2453 B (XXIII) of 20 December 1968, 2601 B (XXIV) of 16 December 1969 and 2733 B (XXV) of 16 December 1970 concerning the elaboration of an agreement on the liability for damage caused by the launching of objects into outer space,

verdict.summary:
FINDING (Ask 1 — verdict)

No. The passage of the supplied text that establishes absolute liability — Article II of the Convention on International Liability for Damage Caused by Space Objects (London/Moscow/Washington, 29 March 1972) — contains no monetary cap. It states no sum, ceiling, formula, index, per-incident or per-claim limit, and it does not refer out to any provision that supplies one. The word 'compensation' appears with no amount attached to it.

VERBATIM PASSAGE RELIED ON (Ask 2 — basis)

Article II, as it appears in the supplied public text (UNOOSA treaty page; FAA reproduction of the Convention; UN Juridical Yearbook 1971, ch. IV; Lovdata treaty database):

    "Article II
    A launching State shall be absolutely liable to pay compensation for damage caused by its space object on the surface of the earth or to aircraft in flight."

Textual note (recorded so the record is not silently cleaned up): the UNOOSA HTML rendering of the same article reads "...or to aircraft flight", omitting "in". That is a rendering/transcription artifact. Every other supplied source — the FAA PDF, the UN Juridical Yearbook PDF, the Lovdata text, and the Springer commentary quoting Article II — reads "aircraft in flight", which is also the reading in Article IV(1)(a) of the same sources. The omission does not affect the answer: with or without "in", the sentence states liability and no amount.

WHAT THE PASSAGE DOES SAY ABOUT LIABILITY (Ask 2 — restatement, confined to the passage)

Element by element, Article II states and states only the following:

1. Who is liable — "A launching State". The bearer of the obligation is the launching State (the term is defined elsewhere in the instrument, in Article I; that definition is not part of this passage and is not restated here).

2. What the standard of liability is — "shall be absolutely liable". Liability is absolute: it is triggered by the causal connection alone. The passage attaches no fault requirement, no negligence requirement, no due-diligence standard, and no burden on the claimant to prove wrongful conduct. This is the respect in which it differs from Article III of the same text, which imposes liability "only if the damage is due to its fault or the fault of persons for whom it is responsible" for damage occurring elsewhere than on the surface of the earth.

3. What the obligation is — "to pay compensation". The obligation is a payment obligation. The passage names the obligation but fixes no quantum.

4. For what — "for damage caused by its space object". The damage must be caused by the launching State's space object. "Damage" is not quantified or capped in this passage.

5. Where — "on the surface of the earth or to aircraft in flight". The absolute standard is geographically and materially bounded: it governs damage on the surface of the earth and damage to aircraft in flight. Article IV(1)(a) of the same text repeats the standard for the third-State case ("their liability to the third State shall be absolute") when the damage is on the surface of the earth or to aircraft in flight.

What the passage does not say, stated expressly because it is the point of the question:

- It does not state a maximum, ceiling, cap, or any figure in any currency.
- It does not state a formula, index, or method for computing an amount.
- It does not incorporate a limit by reference to any other article or instrument.
- It does not condition payment on a fund, insurance, registration, or budgetary appropriation.
- It does not create a presumption, rebuttable or otherwise, as to amount.
- It does not use the words 'limit', 'maximum', 'up to', 'not exceeding', or their equivalents.

CONTEXT EXPRESSLY MARKED AS OUTSIDE THE PASSAGE (not part of the answer to Ask 2)

For completeness of the file, and flagged as context only because the request confines the restatement to the absolute-liability passage:

- Article VI(1) of the same text provides for exoneration from absolute liability to the extent the launching State establishes that the damage resulted from gross negligence or an act or omission done with intent to cause damage by the claimant State or its represented persons. That is a defence to liability, not a cap on amount.
- Article XII of the same text provides that compensation "shall be determined in accordance with international law and the principles of justice and equity, in order to provide such reparation ... as will restore the person ... to the condition which would have existed if the damage had not occurred" — a restoration standard, again with no figure.
- Article XIII addresses the currency of payment; Article XVIII establishes the Claims Commission. None of these supplies a monetary ceiling.
- A secondary commentary in the supplied materials (Springer, on the Liability Convention) states the same conclusion in terms: the Convention "deliberately does not provide for any maximum limit to damages". This is corroboration only; the finding above rests on the primary text.

SCOPE AND LIMITS OF THIS FINDING

This is a finding about the text as supplied. It answers the question 'does this passage state a monetary cap' and 'what does this passage say about liability'. It does not opine on whether a tribunal might in practice arrive at a bounded figure, on how 'damage' or 'launching State' are to be construed in a particular fact pattern, or on the law of any jurisdiction applying the Convention. Those would be questions of application, and would require the relevant instruments and facts to be put in evidence.

verdict.summary:
LEGAL ANALYSIS — MINIMUM NOTICE PERIOD FOR DENUNCIATION/WITHDRAWAL

1. IDENTIFICATION OF THE SUPPLIED TEXT (Ask 1 — constraint)

The supplied UN treaty text is the Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties, adopted 23 May 1969 (UN Doc. A/CONF.39/27; in force 27 January 1980; UNTS vol. 1155, p. 331, No. I-18232). The instrument is identified by three independent markers in the supplied pages: (a) the A/CONF.39/27 conference document carries the Convention's own article numbering and text (Arts. 26–30, 42, 55–57, 65–66); (b) the UNTS vol. 1155, No. I-18232 printing reproduces the same articles with the same wording, confirming the authentic published text; and (c) the depositary handbook (treaties.un.org/doc/source/publications/thb/english.pdf) cites 'article 56 of the Vienna Convention 1969' by name and restates the same rule.

2. THE OPERATIVE PROVISION

Article 56 — 'Denunciation of or withdrawal from a treaty containing no provision regarding termination, denunciation or withdrawal'

Paragraph 1 establishes the threshold question — whether denunciation or withdrawal is available at all where the treaty is silent:
  '1. A treaty which contains no provision regarding its termination and which does not provide for denunciation or withdrawal is not subject to denunciation or withdrawal unless:
  (a) it is established that the parties intended to admit the possibility of denunciation or withdrawal; or
  (b) a right of denunciation or withdrawal may be implied by the nature of the treaty.'

Paragraph 2 states the notice period:
  '2. A party shall give not less than twelve months' notice of its intention to denounce or withdraw from a treaty under paragraph 1.'

3. ANSWER (Ask 2 — value)

Minimum notice period: TWELVE MONTHS (12 months).

The operative words are 'not less than twelve months' notice'. Twelve months is therefore a floor, not a fixed term: a party may give longer notice, but not shorter. The notice is of the party's 'intention to denounce or withdraw', and it runs from the giving of notice; the Convention sets no separate rule here for when the twelve-month clock starts beyond the act of notification itself (contrast Art. 65(2), below).

4. WHY THE CROSS-REFERENCE 'UNDER PARAGRAPH 1' IS THE RIGHT HOOK

The question asks for the period 'under paragraph 1'. Article 56 is structured so that paragraph 1 defines the class of treaties and the conditions in which denunciation/withdrawal is available, and paragraph 2 attaches the twelve-month notice requirement to a denunciation/withdrawal 'under paragraph 1'. The quoted text is unambiguous on this point and no inference or calculation is required. The 1966 ILC draft articles (A/CN.4/199, draft Art. 53(2)) carry the identical sentence, confirming that the twelve-month figure is the settled drafting outcome and not a transcription artifact.

5. SCOPE CAVEATS A REVIEWER SHOULD CARRY WITH THE FIGURE

(a) Article 56 is a residual rule. It governs only where the treaty itself is silent on termination, denunciation or withdrawal. If the treaty in the file contains its own withdrawal clause, that clause supplies the notice period and Art. 56(2) does not apply — Art. 54(a) VCLT permits termination or withdrawal 'in conformity with the provisions of the treaty'. The twelve-month figure answers the question as posed ('under paragraph 1'), i.e. for the Art. 56 case.

(b) Article 54(b) is a separate route — withdrawal at any time by consent of all the parties — to which no notice period attaches.

(c) Article 65(2) is NOT the notice period and must not be confused with it. That provision sets a three-month waiting period, except in cases of special urgency, after receipt of a notification of a claim before the notifying party may carry out the proposed measure. It is a procedural cooling-off period for invoking invalidity/termination/suspension grounds, not the Art. 56(2) notice of intention to denounce. Likewise, the twelve-month period in Art. 66 is the outer limit for triggering the conciliation procedure under Art. 65(3), not a notice period.

(d) The depositary handbook's summary is consistent and may be cited as corroboration: 'In the case of a treaty that is silent on withdrawal or denunciation, by giving at least 12 months' notice... (see article 56 of the Vienna Convention 1969).'

6. VERIFICATION

- Text quoted verbatim from two independent reproductions in the supplied set (A/CONF.39/27 and UNTS vol. 1155, No. I-18232), which agree word for word.
- Figure stated in the answer (12 months) equals the figure in the quoted operative sentence; no rounding, conversion or computation applied.
- No other figure appearing in this analysis (3 months, Art. 65(2); 12 months, Art. 66) is presented as the answer, and each is expressly labelled as a distinct procedural period, so the deliverable contains no internally inconsistent threshold.

asks.quote: what is the sum, in months, of the stated two-month period for agreeing to adopt a conciliation procedure and the stated five-month period after the conciliation commission's appointment for it to make its recommendations?
Add only those two stated periods
do not treat the result as a deadline measured from notification of the dispute

verdict.summary:
Legal basis and calculation:

Article II of the Optional Protocol to the Vienna Convention on Consular Relations concerning the Compulsory Jurisdiction of the International Court of Justice (Vienna, 24 April 1963) provides that the parties concerned may agree to have recourse to a conciliation commission; that the Commission shall be constituted within two months after the date on which one party has notified the other of its intention to have recourse to conciliation; and that the Commission shall make its recommendations within five months after its appointment.

The request asks only for the sum of the two stated periods: the stated two-month period and the stated five-month period.

2 months + 5 months = 7 months.

The result is not a deadline measured from notification of the dispute. The two-month period runs from notification of intention to have recourse to conciliation, while the five-month period runs from the appointment of the Commission. The addition is therefore purely arithmetic and yields 7 months. No other period (such as any period for the President of the International Court of Justice to appoint members if the Commission is not constituted) is added.

Note: The Protocol's two-month period is expressly the period within which the Commission is to be constituted after notification of intention to have recourse to conciliation; the request's shorthand description of it as the period 'for agreeing to adopt a conciliation procedure' does not alter the stated duration of two months.

20 February 2017

Download (993.9 kB)
Overview
This first addendum to the fourth edition of the Guidelines for drinking-water quality (GDWQ) details the changes that have been made to the fourth edition of the GDWQ. Updates reflect new evidence and further, provides additional explanations to support better understanding and application of the guidance.
The key updates in the first addendum include updated or revised risk assessments and/or guideline values or health-based values for barium; bentazone; chlorine dioxide, chlorate and chlorite; dichlorvos; dicofol; diquat; lead; MCPA; nitrate and nitrite; and perchlorate. Additional guidance on risk management considerations and monitoring of lead is provided, alongside new guidance on microbial risk assessment, aggregating multiple barriers for overall water treatment performance and microbial detection methods.

Abstract

Access to safe drinking-water is fundamental to public health, human well-being and sustainable development. This publication presents the fourth edition of the WHO Guidelines for drinking-water quality, incorporating the first addendum, and provides a comprehensive framework for managing risks that may compromise the safety of drinking-water. The Guidelines are intended primarily for regulators, policy-makers and their advisers, supporting the development of national policies, standards and regulations based on preventive risk management from catchment to consumer. They address microbial, chemical, radiological and acceptability aspects of drinking-water quality, together with the roles of surveillance, health-based targets and water safety plans.

The publication further develops concepts introduced in previous editions, including the multiple-barrier approach to drinking-water safety, the application of water safety plans, quantitative risk assessment and guidance for a wide range of supply systems and specific circumstances. It includes updated scientific information, revised and new guideline values and health-based values for selected contaminants, expanded guidance on microbial hazards, climate change, emergency situations and pesticides used for vector control, as well as detailed fact sheets, supporting documentation and practical guidance to facilitate implementation in diverse national and local contexts.

Guidelines for drinking-water quality: fourth edition incorporating the first and second addenda
21 March 2022
| Guideline
Download (5.1 MB)
Overview
The fourth edition incorporating the first and second addenda, of the World Health Organization’s (WHO) Guidelines for drinking-water quality (GDWQ) builds on over 60 years of guidance by WHO on drinking-water quality, which has formed an authoritative basis for the setting of national regulations and standards for water safety in support of public health.
It is the product of significant revisions to clarify and elaborate on ways of implementing its recommendations of contextual hazard identification and risk management, through the establishment of health-based targets, catchment-to-consumer water safety plans and independent surveillance.
Updates in this latest edition reflect new evidence and further, provides additional explanations to support better understanding and application of the guidance. More details on the updates are included in the GDWQ preface.
What is new?

verdict.summary:
COMPLIANCE DETERMINATION — WHO GDWQ page wording (4th edition citation)

1. SCOPE AND SOURCE OF GROUNDING
This determination is made solely from the supplied WHO publication page text for 'Guidelines for drinking-water quality, 4th edition, incorporating the 1st addendum', https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/9789241549950 (fetched 2026-11-23T00:29:26Z, sha256 306abca4bb1f). Corroborating page text is cited where noted. Nothing below is inferred beyond what the page states; where the page is silent, that is recorded as silent rather than filled in.

2. ASK 2 — UPDATED VERSION THE PAGE DIRECTS READERS TO ACCESS
Verbatim, from the page's Overview block:

  "Access here the latest and updated version of this publication: Guidelines for drinking-water quality - Fourth edition incorporating the first and second addenda"

Determination: the page directs readers to the version titled 'Guidelines for drinking-water quality - Fourth edition incorporating the first and second addenda' (the 2022 consolidated version, published at https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/9789240045064, 21 March 2022). The page presents this as 'the latest and updated version of this publication', i.e. as the replacement for the 4th-edition-plus-1st-addendum item the reader is on.

Corroboration (not needed for the answer, recorded for the file): the IRIS record for the 2017 first-addendum volume, https://iris.who.int/handle/10665/254637, carries the note "Updated version with second addendum available here: https://iris.who.int/handle/10665/352532". Both point to the same successor version.

3. ASK 3 — WHAT THE PAGE SAYS THE FIRST ADDENDUM DOES
Verbatim, from the same Overview block:

  "This first addendum updates the fourth edition. Updates reflect new evidence and further, provides additional explanations to support better understanding and application of the guidance."

Determination: the page says the first addendum (a) updates the fourth edition, and (b) that those updates reflect new evidence and provide additional explanations supporting better understanding and application of the guidance. The quoted sentence is reproduced exactly as published, including the page's own grammar ('and further, provides'); it should be quoted, not paraphrased or tidied, in any file that relies on it.

Two further statements on the same page are part of the page's description of the addendum and should travel with it if the file quotes more than the sentence above:
  - "View the detailed list of changes in the first addendum to the fourth edition of the GDWQ" (a link, not a description of effect).
  - The page does not, in the supplied text, itemise which guideline values changed; that detail sits on the separate 1st-addendum page (https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/9789241550017), which states the addendum "details the changes that have been made to the fourth edition" and lists key updates (barium; bentazone; chlorine dioxide, chlorate and chlorite; dichlorvos; dicofol; diquat; lead; MCPA; nitrate and nitrite; perchlorate; plus risk-management/monitoring guidance on lead and new microbial guidance). If the compliance file needs the substance of the changes, cite that page separately; do not attribute its list to the 9789241549950 page.

4. CORRECTION TO APPLY TO THE COMPLIANCE FILE
Current (outdated) wording — cites the bare fourth edition:
  "WHO, Guidelines for drinking-water quality, 4th edition"
Replace with the version the page directs readers to:
  "WHO (2022). Guidelines for drinking-water quality: fourth edition incorporating the first and second addenda. Geneva: World Health Organization. https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/9789240045064"
Where the file also describes the first addendum, use the page's own wording:
  "The first addendum updates the fourth edition; updates reflect new evidence and provide additional explanations to support better understanding and application of the guidance (WHO GDWQ page, https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/9789241549950)."
Rules for applying it:
  - Correct the citation at every occurrence in the file, not only the first, and check the reference list, headers/footers, and any table that names the edition.
  - Do not shorten the title to '4th edition' anywhere; the addenda qualifier is the operative part of the correction.
  - If the file previously cited the 2017 'fourth edition incorporating the first addendum' as current, that citation is also superseded and must move to the first-and-second-addenda version.
  - Retain the old wording only where the file is deliberately describing the historical 2011 text; in that case label it as superseded.

5. VERIFICATION CHECKS RUN AGAINST THIS DELIVERABLE
  - Ask 2 value matches the page's directive sentence word-for-word after the colon; it is the version the page names, not a version I selected.
  - Ask 3 value is a verbatim quotation; it is not a paraphrase and does not import the separate 1st-addendum page's change list.
  - The correction in section 4 cites the same version named in Ask 2; no other version is proposed as the file's citation anywhere in this deliverable.
  - The page's statement is reported as the page's statement; no independent assessment of the guidelines' scientific currency is asserted.

6. OUT-OF-SCOPE OBSERVATION (flagged, does not alter the answers above)
A later consolidated version exists — 'Guidelines for drinking-water quality: fourth edition incorporating the first, second and third addenda' — whose preface states it "supersedes previous editions of the Guidelines, including the fourth edition incorporating the first and second addenda, published in 2022" (https://iris.who.int/server/api/core/bitstreams/c60cc28e-defe-45ed-b157-71fdd43902bf/content). This does not change Ask 2 or Ask 3, which are answered strictly from the supplied page text. It is recorded because a compliance file corrected only to the 2022 version will itself be one revision behind; that is a separate decision for the document owner and should be raised as its own change, not folded silently into this correction.

7. LIMIT OF THIS ROLE'S OUTPUT
This is the written determination and the exact correction text. Applying the edit to the compliance file, and any decision to jump the file straight to the third-addendum version, sit with the document owner; nothing here was executed against any system.

verdict.summary:
RFC 7519 — JSON Web Token (JWT), May 2015 — Section 4 ("JWT Claims"), first paragraph, page 8.

## 1. The exact rule (verbatim)

> The JWT Claims Set represents a JSON object whose members are the
> claims conveyed by the JWT.  The Claim Names within a JWT Claims Set
> MUST be unique; JWT parsers MUST either reject JWTs with duplicate
> Claim Names or use a JSON parser that returns only the lexically last
> duplicate member name, as specified in Section 15.12 ("The JSON
> Object") of ECMAScript 5.1 [ECMAScript].

This text is identical on both mirrors consulted (rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7519.html#section-4 and datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc7519#section-4), word for word. No errata affecting this sentence were found in the sources consulted.

## 2. Normative decomposition

The paragraph contains two distinct MUST-level obligations, one on the producer and one on the consumer. They are not the same obligation, and conflating them is the usual source of error.

| # | Actor | Obligation | Strength |
|---|-------|-----------|----------|
| R1 | Issuer / anyone constructing a JWT Claims Set | Claim Names within a JWT Claims Set MUST be unique — i.e. no two members of the Claims Set JSON object may have equal names. | MUST |
| R2 | JWT parser (relying party) | On encountering a JWT whose Claims Set has duplicate Claim Names, the parser MUST do one of exactly two things: (a) reject the JWT, or (b) use a JSON parser that returns only the **lexically last** duplicate member name. | MUST (choice of two conformant behaviors) |

Key consequences:

1. **A duplicate-name Claims Set is non-conformant to produce.** R1 is a MUST on the producer; there is no "SHOULD" softening. A token with `{"sub":"alice","sub":"bob"}` was produced in violation of RFC 7519 regardless of how the receiver handles it.
2. **The receiver is not required to reject.** RFC 7519 does not mandate rejection. Either rejecting or last-wins resolution is conformant. This is an explicit either/or, and both branches are equally valid per the spec.
3. **"Lexically last" means last in the serialized JSON text**, i.e. the rightmost occurrence in document order of the member name within that object — *not* lexicographically greatest by string comparison. The phrase anchors to ECMAScript 5.1 §15.12 ("The JSON Object"), which specifies that when an object literal / parsed object contains repeated names, the last occurrence's value is the one that survives (`JSON.parse('{"a":1,"a":2}')` yields `{a: 2}`).
4. **"Returns only" is significant.** Branch (b) requires the parser to *collapse* duplicates to a single member whose value is the last one; a parser that surfaces both occurrences (e.g. as a multi-map or an array of pairs) and leaves the choice to application code does not satisfy branch (b) — such a parser must instead take branch (a) and reject.
5. **Scope: the Claims Set only.** Section 4 governs the JWT Claims Set (the JWS Payload / JWE plaintext). The rule does not by its own words govern the JOSE Header; JOSE header parameter uniqueness is handled by the JWS/JWE specifications. A separate and unrelated concept is the *replicated claims* mechanism of Section 5.2 ("Replicating Claims as Header Parameters"), where `iss`/`sub`/`aud` may appear both as header parameters and as claims; RFC 7519 says the receiver SHOULD verify those replicated values are identical — that is a cross-structure consistency check, not the intra-Claims-Set duplicate rule.
6. **Scope: not cryptographic validation.** This is a structural/syntactic acceptance rule applied when the Claims Set JSON is parsed. It is orthogonal to signature/MAC verification (Section 7.2) and to the string-comparison rules (Section 7.3), which govern how known names/values are matched against parsed members.
7. **Relationship to plain JSON.** RFC 7159 §4 (and RFC 8259 §4) only says object names *SHOULD* be unique. RFC 7519 tightens this to *MUST* for the JWT Claims Set and additionally imposes a receiver-side MUST, which base JSON does not.

## 3. Context from Section 3 (JWT Overview)

Section 3 establishes the vocabulary that Section 4's rule operates on:

> JWTs represent a set of claims as a JSON object that is encoded in a JWS and/or JWE structure.  This JSON object is the JWT Claims Set. [...] The member names within the JWT Claims Set are referred to as Claim Names.  The corresponding values are referred to as Claim Values.

So "duplicate Claim Names" = two or more members of the Claims Set JSON object whose name strings are equal under the JSON string-comparison rules of RFC 7159 §8.3 (referenced by RFC 7519 §7.3). Equality is exact string equality after JSON unescaping — e.g. `"sub"` and `"\u0073ub"` denote the same Claim Name and therefore count as duplicates, whereas `"sub"` and `"Sub"` do not.

## 4. Implementation guidance (parser side)

To be conformant, a JWT parser must be *deterministically* in one branch. Pick one and document it:

**Branch (a) — reject on duplicates (recommended for security-sensitive verifiers):**

```text
function parseClaimsSet(bytes) -> ClaimsSet | Error:
    seen = set()
    for (name, value) in streaming_json_members(bytes):
        if name in seen:
            return Error("duplicate Claim Name: " + name)   # RFC 7519 §4 branch (a)
        seen.add(name)
        claims[name] = value
    return claims
```

Requirements for branch (a): the JSON reader must expose *every* member, including repeats. Most default parsers (Python `json`, Go `encoding/json` into `map[string]interface{}`, JavaScript `JSON.parse`) silently collapse duplicates and therefore **cannot** implement branch (a) as-is; you need a streaming/hook-based reader (`object_pairs_hook` in Python, a custom `UnmarshalJSON`, a SAX-style tokenizer, or a duplicate-detecting decoder).

**Branch (b) — last-occurrence-wins, as ECMAScript 5.1 §15.12:**

```text
function parseClaimsSet(bytes) -> ClaimsSet:
    claims = {}
    for (name, value) in streaming_json_members(bytes):   # document order
        claims[name] = value        # later assignment overwrites: last one wins
    return claims
```

This is what a plain `JSON.parse` / `json.loads` / `map[string]interface{}` decode gives you, and it is conformant *provided* you accept that the surviving value is the one from the last textual occurrence.

**Non-conformant middle ground to avoid:** parsing into a structure that retains all duplicates and then applying ad-hoc precedence rules (first-wins, merge, error-on-use) — that is neither branch (a) nor branch (b).

**Producer side (R1):** serialize the Claims Set from a data structure that cannot hold duplicate keys (a map/dict/object) so uniqueness holds by construction. If you accept user-supplied claim names, reject or de-duplicate at claim-construction time rather than emitting a token that violates the MUST.

## 5. One-sentence answer

RFC 7519 §4 requires that Claim Names within a JWT Claims Set MUST be unique, and requires a JWT parser that receives duplicate Claim Names to either reject the JWT outright or use a JSON parser that keeps only the lexically last duplicate member name (per ECMAScript 5.1 §15.12).

draft-ietf-jose-deprecate-none-rsa15-08
Abstract
This document updates RFC 7518 (JSON Web Algorithms (JWA)) to
deprecate the JSON Web Signature (JWS) algorithm "none" and the JSON
Web Encryption (JWE) algorithm "RSA1_5".  These algorithms have known
security weaknesses.  It updates RFC 7519 (JSON Web Token (JWT)) so
that these two algorithms are no longer mandatory to implement.  It
also updates the review instructions for Designated Experts to
establish baseline security requirements that future algorithm
registrations are expected to meet.

verdict.summary:
## Answer

Per RFC 7519 §8 ("Implementation Requirements"), exactly two of the JWS signature/MAC algorithm identifiers registered in JSON Web Algorithms (RFC 7518) are mandatory to implement for conforming JWT implementations:

- **`HS256`** — HMAC using SHA-256 (a MAC algorithm)
- **`none`** — no digital signature or MAC performed (the unsecured JWS case)

Everything else is at most RECOMMENDED or OPTIONAL.

### Normative text (RFC 7519 §8, verbatim)

> "Of the signature and MAC algorithms specified in JSON Web Algorithms [JWA], only HMAC SHA-256 ("HS256") and "none" MUST be implemented by conforming JWT implementations. It is RECOMMENDED that implementations also support RSASSA-PKCS1-v1_5 with the SHA-256 hash algorithm ("RS256") and ECDSA using the P-256 curve and the SHA-256 hash algorithm ("ES256"). Support for other algorithms and key sizes is OPTIONAL."

This sentence is the single clause carrying the MUST; it is the whole answer to the question. The same paragraph also permits applications to raise the bar: "Applications using this specification can impose additional requirements upon implementations that they use" (e.g., an application profile may make `ES256` or `RS256` mandatory for its own participants — that is an application requirement, not a JWT conformance requirement).

### Scope resolution (ask 1)

- **In scope:** JWS algorithms in RFC 7518 §3 — §3.2 HMAC (MAC), §3.3 RSASSA-PKCS1-v1_5 (signature), §3.4 ECDSA (signature), §3.5 RSASSA-PSS (signature), §3.6 `none`.
- **Out of scope:** JWE key-management and content-encryption algorithms (RFC 7518 §4, §5), which RFC 7519 §8 handles in a separate, conditional sentence ("If an implementation provides encryption capabilities..." `RSA1_5`, `A128KW`, `A256KW`, `A128CBC-HS256`, `A256CBC-HS512`). Encryption is OPTIONAL for JWTs and therefore not part of this answer.
- **Note on `none`:** strictly, `none` is neither a signature nor a MAC algorithm — it is the marker for an unsecured JWS. RFC 7519 nevertheless counts it inside the "signature and MAC algorithms" sentence, and RFC 7518 §3.1 lists it with implementation requirement **Required**. So a conforming JWT implementation must *implement* `none` (i.e., be able to produce/parse an unsecured JWT per JWS §6), but that is a far cry from being permitted to *accept* it in a security context — see "MUST implement ≠ MUST accept" below.

### Full JWS algorithm inventory with implementation requirements (RFC 7518 §3.1 table)

| `alg` | Type | Algorithm | RFC 7518 requirement | RFC 7519 §8 status |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `HS256` | MAC | HMAC using SHA-256 | **Required** | **MUST implement** |
| `HS384` | MAC | HMAC using SHA-384 | Optional | OPTIONAL |
| `HS512` | MAC | HMAC using SHA-512 | Optional | OPTIONAL |
| `RS256` | Signature | RSASSA-PKCS1-v1_5 using SHA-256 | Recommended | RECOMMENDED |
| `RS384` | Signature | RSASSA-PKCS1-v1_5 using SHA-384 | Optional | OPTIONAL |
| `RS512` | Signature | RSASSA-PKCS1-v1_5 using SHA-512 | Optional | OPTIONAL |
| `ES256` | Signature | ECDSA using P-256 and SHA-256 | Recommended | RECOMMENDED |
| `ES384` | Signature | ECDSA using P-384 and SHA-384 | Optional | OPTIONAL |
| `ES512` | Signature | ECDSA using P-521 and SHA-512 | Optional | OPTIONAL |
| `PS256` | Signature | RSASSA-PSS using SHA-256, MGF1-SHA-256 | Optional | OPTIONAL |
| `PS384` | Signature | RSASSA-PSS using SHA-384, MGF1-SHA-384 | Optional | OPTIONAL |
| `PS512` | Signature | RSASSA-PSS using SHA-512, MGF1-SHA-512 | Optional | OPTIONAL |
| `none` | — | No digital signature or MAC performed | **Required** | **MUST implement** |

The `HS256`/`HS384`/`HS512` rows above are directly corroborated by the fetched RFC 7518 text ("HS256 | HMAC using SHA-256 | Required", "HS384 ... Optional", "HS512 ... Optional"); `RS256` and `ES256` are corroborated by the explicit RECOMMENDED sentence in RFC 7519 §8.

### Two distinctions that matter operationally

1. **Mandatory-to-implement vs mandatory-to-use/accept.** A MUST-implement requirement is a *capability* floor, not a policy. RFC 7519 §8 does not require an implementation to *accept* `none` or `HS256` in any given context; RFC 8725 (JWT BCP) and RFC 7519 §11/§12 security considerations point the other way — reject `none` unless explicitly configured, pin the accepted algorithm set per issuer/key, never let the `alg` header select the verification key type, and compare MACs in constant time (RFC 7518 §3.2: "The comparison of the computed HMAC value to the JWS Signature value MUST be done in a constant-time manner to thwart timing attacks").
2. **`HS256` key floor.** RFC 7518 §3.2 requires a key of at least the hash output size (256 bits for `HS256`), so a conforming `HS256` implementation must reject shorter secrets rather than silently accept them.

### Version/errata caveat (important for anyone citing this answer)

As of the current IETF document set, `none` is still mandatory to implement per the published RFC 7519. A draft, `draft-ietf-jose-deprecate-none-rsa15` ("JOSE: Deprecate 'none' and 'RSA1_5'", fetched at revision -08, dated 1 November 2026, "Updates: 7518, 7519 (if approved)"), would remove that: "This document updates [RFC7519] to remove both requirements: 'none' and 'RSA1_5' are no longer mandatory to implement for conforming JWT implementations." Because it is an Internet-Draft and not an RFC, the correct answer *today* remains **`HS256` and `none`**; if/when that draft is published as an RFC, the answer becomes **`HS256`** alone. Any compliance checklist built on this answer should record the RFC 7519 publication date (May 2015) and the applicable-updates status so the assumption is auditable.

### Conformance check a backend implementation can run

1. `HS256` sign and verify against RFC 7515 Appendix A.1 test vector (JWS Signing Input / key / expected signature); confirm constant-time comparison is used.
2. `HS256` key-length validation: 32-byte key accepted, 16-byte key rejected.
3. `none` handling: parse and (when the profile permits) emit an unsecured JWT with an empty signature segment and `"alg":"none"`; confirm the default verification path rejects `none`.
4. Negative: `HS384`, `HS512`, `RS256`, `ES256`, `PS256` may be absent from a minimal conforming build without loss of JWT conformance (they are Recommended/Optional), though most production profiles will require at least `RS256` or `ES256` by application policy.

### Sources

- RFC 7519 §8, "Implementation Requirements" (May 2015) — the quoted MUST sentence; also §11/§12 security considerations.
- RFC 7518 §3.1 (JWS algorithm requirements table), §3.2 (HMAC, key-size floor, constant-time comparison), §3.6 (`none`).
- `draft-ietf-jose-deprecate-none-rsa15` §6 — pending removal of the `none` requirement (not yet an RFC).
- RFC 8725 (JWT BCP) — algorithm pinning and `none` rejection guidance, referenced for the implement-vs-accept distinction.

7.2.  JWS JSON Serialization
The JWS JSON Serialization represents digitally signed or MACed
content as a JSON object.  This representation is neither optimized
for compactness nor URL-safe.
Two closely related syntaxes are defined for the JWS JSON
Serialization: a fully general syntax, with which content can be
secured with more than one digital signature and/or MAC operation,
and a flattened syntax, which is optimized for the single digital
signature or MAC case.

"signature":"<signature contents>"
}

5.1 Message Signature or MAC Computation​
To create a JWS, the following steps are performed. The order of the steps is not significant in cases where there are no dependencies between the inputs and outputs of the steps.
Create the content to be used as the JWS Payload.
Compute the encoded payload value BASE64URL(JWS Payload).
Create the JSON object(s) containing the desired set of Header Parameters, which together comprise the JOSE Header (the JWS Protected Header and/or the JWS Unprotected Header).
